newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Sea-borne saboteurs seen threat to South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Sea-borne saboteurs seen threat to South Korea.

text.p: South Korea faces a threat of sea-borne saboteurs, but Washington will send aircraft carriers to defend the country if war breaks out on the peninsula, a senior U.S. military official said on Thursday.

Rear Admiral Chales Moore, commander of the battle group of the U.S. aircraft carrier Independence, said part of the current U.S.-South Korean military exercise was intended to hone skills to intercept submarines carrying North Korean commandos.
A submarine from the communist North intruded into South Korea last month, heightening tension on the Korean peninsula, the world's last cold war frontier.
Moore said the annual joint military exercise, codenamed "Foal Eagle '96", would train U.S. and South Korean troops to cope with "every dimension of warfare".
"Korea is a unique theatre," he told reporters aboard the Independence. "We do not see too many places around the world where special operations forces infiltrate by sea."

"Foal Eagle is a rare opportunity for us to hone our skills -- going after small, hard-to-detect, high-speed manoeuvrable craft that would be carrying SOP (special operations) forces in submarines," he said.
The two-week exercise involves some 34,000 U.S. troops, including 10,000 seamen from the U.S. Seventh Fleet, and most of South Korea's 655,000 military personnel.

North Korea's Shark-class submarine ran aground off the eastern city of Kangnung on September 17 as it tried to pick up three spies it had delivered two days earlier, according to the only North Korean captured alive from the vessel.
It lay stuck on rocks unnoticed by South Korean security forces until an alert taxi driver spotted the coning tower of the vessel looming out of the waters the following day.
By then, 26 North Koreans involved in the submarine mission had fled to the hills, where 22 have been shot dead. A hunt is underway for three missing intruders.
"Our goal in Foal Eagle is to try to replicate those missions that we feel we are required to perform in the event of war," said Moore, whose battle group exercised off the east coast.
"It is clear in the event of war, carrier battle groups would be deployed to this theatre and would participate," he said.

Moore said the Independence, which is based in Japan, would probably be the first U.S. aircraft carrier sent to Korea to defend against any North Korean attack unless it was enganged in another conflict or under maintenance.
"We would be the first, and rapidly in succession others would come as they are deployed from the United States."
The South Korean Defence Ministry, which mobilised 40,000 soldiers to hunt for the North Koreans from the submarine, said the incursion was preparation for wider military provocation.
Captured North Korean Lee Kwang-soo, a coxswain, told reporters on Tuesday that his submarine had little difficulty slipping through South Korean coastal defences.
The incursion rattled South Koreans led to charges that the military was getting complacent against the North Korean security threat.
The captured North Korean said of South Korean coastal defences against northern infiltration: "If you come in by a submarine you can do it as many times as you like."
